children: By Emma Tucker
From My Desk

John Fetterman's blue-collar wardrobe and plain-spoken progressivism once made him a star. Now, the Pennsylvania senator is showing little interest in doing his job beyond cultivating relationships with conservative media figures and advocating for Israel. Interviews with more than a dozen former aides and lawmakers, along with internal records, show an increasingly dysfunctional operation as Fetterman churns through staff and dodges constituents. With a pivotal election looming that could give him outsize influence in Congress, Will Hobson and Siobhan Hughes report on the senator's shifting politics — and his growing distance from fellow Democrats.

Read It Here First
War is ruining the year for the wealthy Arab Gulf.

When war arrived in the Middle East this year, Gulf leaders pinned their hopes on a brief conflict, expecting to roar back by the fall and end a disastrous period in their history. Instead, they are writing the year off as a loss, according to people familiar with their thinking, as fighting between the U.S. and Iran drags into its seventh month and a bleak economic picture descends on the region. Marquee events have been disrupted, and luxury hotels are largely empty and slashing staff as war risks keep air travelers away, report Omar Abdel-Baqui and Summer Said.
The American dream is alive — and minting millionaires.

Pop culture portrays the rich as an elite few, akin to the Rockefellers and Carnegies of the Gilded Age. But as economists Owen Zidar and Eric Zwick write in an essay adapted from their book, "The Everywhere Millionaire," rich private business owners are now so plentiful that America has entered its first Age of Millionaires. You probably know an Everywhere Millionaire, even if you don't realize it. They're hiding in plain sight: ordinary people running businesses woven into the fabric of daily life, from restaurant chains to HVAC services — and proving that an elite degree isn't a prerequisite for building massive wealth.
See The Story
These $400,000 keys get you onto Martha's Vineyard's private beaches.

On Martha's Vineyard, "beach keys" are the ultimate status symbol, giving affluent property owners entry to secluded stretches of sand that are off-limits to the masses. Keys come with deeded ownership to a sliver of non-buildable beachfront. They often stay in the same family for generations, though a handful sell on the open market each year. Prices for these keys have shot up in recent years thanks to wealthy buyers — seemingly undeterred by the threat of erosion — clamoring for privacy and convenience amid the island's swelling popularity. Last year, one sold for $650,000.

Number Of The Day
$13 billion

The rough amount Nvidia agreed to pay for Hugging Face, an open-source AI platform that began as a sassy chatbot for teens. Founded in 2016 by a trio of nerdy Frenchmen and named after their favorite emoji, the startup has grown into a vital pillar of the tech ecosystem.
And Finally. . .
Starbucks refreshed its menu. Chai fans are losing their minds.

The company is on a mission to boost sales, and CEO Brian Niccol has been rethinking everything. The coffee chain's new "premium chai" recipe reflects a fresh focus on customization, sweetened with just two grams of honey so customers can adjust flavor. Regulars aren't buying it. The company's loyal tea drinkers are emailing executives and signing petitions in a desperate bid to bring back the old recipe — and get to the bottom of the "Great Chai Incident of 2026."
